articles.title: Same config.json, different serve command: what to check before serving AREX-2
articles.excerpt: When a fine-tune declares the same architecture class as a model you already serve (run behind an API on your own GPU), the tempting move is to swap --model-path and restart. BAAI's AREX-2 is a good t…
articles.body: When a fine-tune declares the same architecture class as a model you already serve (run behind an API on your own GPU), the tempting move is to swap --model-path and restart. BAAI's AREX-2 is a good test of that habit. It is a 27B model trained to work on a problem in rounds (propose, measure, reflect, revise), released on 29 September under Apache 2.0, not gated, and its config.json opens with Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration , the same class as Qwen3.8-27B from the Qwen team. We had been serving base Qwen3.8-27B with sglang, an open-source inference server, so we diffed the two configs. One caveat first: we have not run AREX-2. Every speed below is from the base model. Tables, command and sources are in the full AREX-2 serving analysis on inferencekey.com .

articles.title: 1Z0-078 Lists RAC First, but Your Cluster Is Built from the Bottom Up
articles.excerpt: If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid…
articles.body: If you run Oracle databases on more than one server, you already know the order things happen in on a real cluster. Someone prepares the operating system, the shared disks and the networks. Then Grid Infrastructure goes on, which brings Oracle Clusterware and Oracle Automatic Storage Management with it. Only after that does anyone install the database software, and only after that does a RAC database exist to tune, patch and connect to. Oracle's exam page for 1Z0-078 lists the same material in the opposite order. It starts with RAC databases and architecture, moves on to Grid Infrastructure in the middle, and ends with ASM disk groups, files and the ASM Cluster File System. That is a fine way to describe a job.

articles.excerpt: What I Built Handling client receipts and expense invoices is tedious, manual, and privacy-sensitive. Freelancers often hesitate to upload sensitive financial documents containing client names, tax ID…
articles.body: What I Built I built LocalFolio, an offline-first invoice and receipt organizer specifically designed for freelancers, independent contractors, and sole proprietors. Handling client receipts and expense invoices is tedious, manual, and privacy-sensitive. Freelancers often hesitate to upload sensitive financial documents containing client names, tax IDs, and bank details to cloud-based proprietary APIs. LocalFolio solves this by running entirely on the user's local machine. It ingests messy folders of PDFs, screenshots, and scans, uses a local vision-language model to extract structured metadata (vendor, date, total amount, category, and tax status), and automatically sorts them into clean, structured folder hierarchies with a fully searchable SQLite ledger.

articles.title: software guard extensions (sgx)
articles.excerpt: Hardware-Enforced Trust Traditional system security assumes the OS kernel (Ring 0) is fully trusted. However, in modern cloud deployments or compromised endpoints, a malicious kernel, rogue administra…
articles.body: Hardware-Enforced Trust What is sgx? Traditional system security assumes the OS kernel (Ring 0) is fully trusted. However, in modern cloud deployments or compromised endpoints, a malicious kernel, rogue administrator, or hypervisor exploit can easily inspect application memory. To eliminate this dependency, security architecture must drop below software abstractions and anchor trust directly in silicon. Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) achieves this by carving out isolated execution units called enclaves , ensuring that even an attacker with root or kernel privileges cannot read application memory. Why sgx? Architectural Trade-offs: Why Enclaves Over Full VMs?

articles.title: I Built a Faceless Video Factory That Remembers Which Content Actually Pays
articles.excerpt: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle My side hustle is faceless short-form video. The problem with every tool I tried: they're script runners. Same t…
articles.body: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle My side hustle is faceless short-form video. The problem with every tool I tried: they're script runners. Same topic list, same output, run after run. Nothing learns. So I built one that does — a factory that remembers what earned money and steers the next video toward it. The loop nobody closes Here's the insight that made this worth building. A faceless-content pipeline has two halves, and everyone only builds the first: Produce a video from a topic (script → render → post) Learn which topics paid, so the next one is better Half 2 is where the money compounds, and it's the half everyone skips.

As is now the norm, basic cybersecurity would have prevented it. French authorities say the systems, made up of entire fleets of refrigerators and freezers throughout a store, were hacked. More specifically, Internet-connected controllers that allow technicians to remotely administer the store-wide systems were compromised. The unknown attackers responsible then activated defrosters long enough for the fridges to reach temperatures as high as 50° Celsius (122° Fahrenheit).

articles.title: Planetary genealogy: Milky Way worlds belong to 1 of 2 ‘families,’ scientists find
articles.excerpt: Scientists have performed a cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems.
articles.body: You can tell a lot about how a child will age by looking at their parents, and it turns out that this could be true for planetary systems, too. Scientists have performed cosmic genealogy on planetary systems in the Milky Way, finding two distinct families that influence the evolution and fate of these systems. The study team, led by researchers at the Italian National Institute for Astrophysics (INAF), studied 300 of the best-understood multiplanet systems of the over 1,000 that astronomers have discovered in the Milky Way. The team's research clarifies how the environments around infant stars directly affect planetary fates and, in turn, the survival of extrasolar planets, or exoplanets , that are potentially capable of hosting life.

articles.title: 'Dungeon Crawler Carl' author Matt Dinniman talks inspirations, success, and the upcoming Peacock TV series (interview)
articles.excerpt: 'Luckily I’m still in love with this story, and I am in love with writing it.'
articles.body: Fall has officially arrived, and as autumn leaves blaze in vivid colors, there is no better time to plunge into the imaginative world of New York Times best-selling author Matt Dinniman's "Dungeon Crawler Carl", the wildly addictive science fantasy book series that's taking the world by storm. Even if you haven't read them, you've probably seen folks carrying these books, emblazoned with their loud, neon-colored covers, at your neighborhood coffee house. You'll see it even more in the future, too, as a streaming adaptation of the novels is coming to Peacock, with Seth MacFarlane's Fuzzy Door and co-showrunners Eric Heisserer and Chris Yost at the helm.

articles.title: The AI race is back on
articles.excerpt: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves,…
articles.body: Mark Zuckerberg at the Meta Connect developer conference. | Photo: Andrej Sokolow/dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images Last week, Anthropic and OpenAI looked like they had the AI race to themselves, pulling ahead with increasingly powerful models that left their rivals in the dust. Google seemed hopelessly far behind, while Meta, despite spending billions to revive its floundering AI ambitions , had yet to establish itself as a serious contender. Even the latest models coming out of China , impressive as they were, appeared to be playing catch-up. Then, in the space of a few days, everything changed. Google and Meta both unveiled frontier models they claim can go toe to toe with the best from OpenAI and Anthropic.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
